claim: The unfavorable count (presence of 5 or more CTCs per 7.5 ml peripheral blood) was associated with poor overall survival in patients with prostate cancer.

evidence.quote: Median OS for men with 5 or more CTCs per 7.5 mL was 27.9 months (95% CI, 24.1-31.2 months) compared with 56.2 months (95% CI, 45.7-69.8 months) for men with 1 to 4 CTCs per 7.5 mL and not reached at 78.0 months follow-up for men with 0 CTCs per 7.5 mL.
evidence.note: 5 or more CTCs per 7.5 mL linked to shorter overall survival in mHSPC. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Prostate cancer population not named in quote.

evidence.quote: The higher baseline CTC count of ≥5 CTC/7.5 mL was associated with worse OS (median, 10.1 v 32.9 months; P = .00568).
evidence.note: Baseline CTC count of 5 or more per 7.5 mL associated with worse OS in CRPC. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Prostate cancer not stated.

claim: The vasculature induced by cancer cells is crooked, leaky and constantly reconfigured.

evidence.quote: Here, I review emerging evidence supporting an alternative hypothesis-that certain antiangiogenic agents can also transiently "normalize" the abnormal structure and function of tumor vasculature to make it more efficient for oxygen and drug delivery.
evidence.note: Says tumor vasculature has abnormal structure and function; leakiness and reconfiguration not stated.

claim: Experimental and clinical evidence suggests that the process of metastasis is also angiogenesis dependent.

evidence.quote: The evident association between the angiogenic and migratory capacities of PDTOs and their clinical metastatic outcomes underscores the potential of the innovative platform for evaluating tumor metastasis, thus offering valuable insights for clinical decision-making.
evidence.note: Reports association between angiogenic capacity and metastatic outcome in organoids; not dependence.

claim: The basement membrane thickness of tumor blood vessels is uneven and the association between pericytes and tumor endothelial cells is weak, leading to vascular leakiness.

evidence.quote: These mice had: (1) reduced pericyte coverage of tumour blood vessels; (2) reduced tumour blood vessel stability; (3) increased blood vessel diameter; (4) enhanced blood vessel leakiness, and (5) abnormal blood vessel basement membrane architecture.
evidence.note: Pericyte-deficient mouse tumors show reduced coverage, leakiness, abnormal basement membrane; uneven thickness not stated.

evidence.quote: In the tumor microenvironment (TME), PC detachment and ablation from tumor microvessels obliterate the vascular integrity and the protective barrier of the vessel wall, leading to increased permeability for cancer cell intravasation.
evidence.note: Pericyte detachment from tumor microvessels increases permeability; basement membrane thickness not addressed.

claim: Tumor angiogenesis is essential for tumor progression.

evidence.quote: Tumours can obtain nutrients and oxygen required to progress and metastasize through the blood supply1.
evidence.note: Tumor progression depends on blood supply; angiogenesis itself introduced in the next sentence.

evidence.quote: For metastasis to take place, many mechanisms are required: angiogenesis, matrix degradation, cell migration, evasion of host immune response and metastatic colonization.
evidence.note: Angiogenesis listed as required for metastasis, a part of progression.

claim: Tumor endothelial cells are irregular monolayers, have a higher expression of proangiogenic factors, and impaired endothelial barrier function when compared with their normal counterparts.

evidence.quote: As examples, TECs show cytogenetic abnormalities, resistance to anticancer drugs, activated proliferation and migration, and specific gene expression patterns.
evidence.note: TECs differ from normal cells in phenotype and gene expression; monolayer shape and barrier function not stated.

evidence.quote: TECs have various features that distinguish them from normal endothelial cells, which include alterations in gene expression patterns, higher angiogenic and metabolic activities, and drug resistance tendencies.
evidence.note: Higher angiogenic activity and altered gene expression in TECs; no barrier function or morphology.

claim: VEGF is highly expressed in tumor endothelial cells (TECs), and because VEGF is a known factor to enhance permeability of blood vessels, tumor blood vessels typically are leaky and immature structures.

evidence.quote: The high pro-angiogenic nature of the TME perpetuates the chaotic network of structurally immature, low pericyte-covered vessels characteristic of the tumor vasculature.
evidence.note: Tumor vessels are immature and low in pericyte coverage; VEGF expression in TECs and leakiness not stated.

evidence.quote: A possible role for VEGF in the targeting of tumor neovasculature has been postulated, based on the overexpression of VEGF receptors in tumor endothelial cells.
evidence.note: VEGF receptors, not VEGF itself, overexpressed in tumor endothelial cells; permeability role only hypothesized.

claim: Integrin α3β1 is involved in breast cancer cell migration and invasion by regulating the production of MMP-2.

evidence.quote: Ligation of the alpha3beta1-tetraspanin protein complexes with monoclonal antibodies specifically stimulates production of matrix metalloproteinase 2 (MMP-2) and induces formation of long invasive protrusions within Matrigel.
evidence.note: alpha3beta1 complexes stimulate MMP-2 production and invasive protrusions in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Breast cancer cells and integrin alpha3beta1 role in migration not stated.

claim: Integrins αVβ3 and αVβ5 are involved in bone sialoprotein-induced cancer cell adhesion, proliferation and migration.

evidence.quote: Experiments with integrin-blocking antibodies demonstrated that BSP-RGD-induced migration utilizes the alpha(v)beta3 vitronectin receptor, whereas adhesion and proliferation responses were alpha(v)beta5-mediated.
evidence.note: alphaVbeta3 mediates migration; alphaVbeta5 mediates adhesion and proliferation in BSP-RGD response. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Quote does not state cancer cells; adhesion/proliferation/migration are BSP-RGD responses by unspecified cells.

evidence.quote: The present results demonstrated that BSP-induced cancer cell adhesion occurs through the binding of the RGD sequence of BSP to the cell integrin receptors αvβ3 and αvβ5.
evidence.note: Both integrins mediate BSP-induced cancer cell adhesion. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Involvement in proliferation and migration; quote covers adhesion only.

claim: A critical aspect of CAF activation involves metabolic reprogramming, particularly the phenomenon known as the "reverse Warburg effect.

evidence.quote: Based on this, a 'dual‑chamber' model, also known as the 'Reverse Warburg effect', is proposed.
evidence.note: Review names the CAF/cancer cell metabolic model the 'Reverse Warburg effect'. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Does not state CAF activation involves metabolic reprogramming; only names a dual-chamber model.

claim: CAFs can originate from the activation and differentiation of quiescent fibroblasts, bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells, and epithelial and endothelial cells.

evidence.quote: Moreover, minor CAF components represent the alternative origin from other TME components (e.g., endothelia and macrophages).
evidence.note: one instance: endothelial (and macrophage) origin of minor CAF components; other claimed origins not stated.

evidence.quote: In colorectal carcinogenesis, pericryptal Lepr-lineage cells proliferate to generate MCAM+ CAFs that shape the tumor-promoting immune microenvironment.
evidence.note: one instance: CAFs arise from Lepr-lineage cells in colorectal cancer; not one of the listed cell types.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) represent one of the most abundant and functionally important components of the tumor stroma.

evidence.quote: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are the most abundant components of the tumor microenvironment.
evidence.note: States CAF abundance in tumor microenvironment (breast cancer review). Strict re-read: the quote does not state 'Functionally important' component not stated; only most abundant.

evidence.quote: Cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) are a central component of the tumor microenvironment and play critical roles in cancer progression and therapeutic response.
evidence.note: States CAFs are central and play critical roles in cancer progression. Strict re-read: the quote does not state 'Most abundant' component of stroma not stated.

claim: Cancer cells can change the microenvironment, which in turn can affect how cancer grows and spreads.

evidence.quote: Tumor metastasis requires systemic remodeling of distant organ microenvironments that impacts immune cell phenotypes, population structure, and intercellular communication.
evidence.note: Metastasis requires microenvironment remodeling; does not say tumor cells do the remodeling or address growth.

evidence.quote: Just as the nervous system can regulate cancer progression, cancer also remodels and hijacks nervous system structure and function.
evidence.note: Cancer remodels nervous system in its environment, which influences progression; narrower than general claim.

claim: Fibroblast assays are currently being studied as a means of predicting how normal tissue may respond to radiation therapy in cancer patients and others.

evidence.quote: In our material, the intrinsic radiosensitivity of head and neck SCC cells could in most cases be predicted from the intrinsic radiosensitivity of dermal fibroblasts established from the same individual.
evidence.note: Fibroblast radiosensitivity used to predict tumor-cell, not normal-tissue, radiosensitivity.

claim: Genetic alterations that result in the deactivation of caveolin-1 (Cav-1) expression lead to autophagy and aerobic glycolysis in cancer-associated fibroblasts.

evidence.quote: PDGFR-β/Cav-1 enhanced glycolysis in CAFs via autophagy-mediated metabolic reprogramming, resulting in increased lactate export that promoted breast cancer cell growth.
evidence.note: Links Cav-1 to CAF autophagy and glycolysis, but via PDGFR-β/Cav-1 activity, not gene deactivation.

claim: IL-4 and IL-13 produced by Th2 cells or by eosinophils elicit alternative M2 polarization of macrophages, which results in tumour promotion.

evidence.quote: Interferon γ (IFN-γ), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induce a classical activation of macrophages (M1), whereas IL-4 and IL-13 induce an alternative activation program in macrophages (M2).
evidence.note: IL-4 and IL-13 induce alternative M2 activation; no Th2/eosinophil source or tumour promotion stated.

evidence.quote: M2 type TAM promoted DNA methylation in LLC-1 cells and LLC-1 cell-bearing mice, which is related to the intensified EZH2.
evidence.note: Shows IL-4/IL-13-induced M2 TAM promote lung cancer cell metastasis and growth; no Th2 or eosinophil source.

claim: Several studies indicate that tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) usually have a pro-tumoral action, since they can stimulate angiogenesis, increase tumor cell invasion and motility, and have an immunosuppressive action.

evidence.quote: TAMs predominantly play a M2-like tumor-promoting role in the TME and regulate various malignant effects, such as angiogenesis, immune suppression, and tumor metastasis; hence, TAMs have emerged as a hot topic of research in cancer therapy.
evidence.note: TAMs predominantly tumor-promoting, regulating angiogenesis, immune suppression and metastasis.

evidence.quote: This M2-TAM bias in the TME promotes cancer cell proliferation, neoangiogenesis, lymphangiogenesis, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, matrix remodeling for metastatic support, and TME manipulation to an immunosuppressive state.
evidence.note: Pro-tumor M2-TAM promotes angiogenesis, metastasis support and immunosuppression; 'usually' is framed via M2 bias.

claim: VEGF-A (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor-A) expression is greatly stimulated by tissue hypoxia and, perhaps independently, by low tissue pH, conditions that are commonly present in the tumor microenvironment.

evidence.quote: Overexpression of HIFs, whether linked to anemia or not, was associated with a number of factors related to tumor aggressiveness (assessed as local invasion and nodal metastasis), anaerobic metabolism and intratumoral acidosis (LDH5, GLUT1; increased glucose metabolism to lactate), activation of genes related to necrosis (BNIP3) and angiogenesis (VEGF).
evidence.note: Hypoxia-pathway (HIF) overexpression associated with VEGF activation; low pH effect on VEGF not stated.

module: 14.2 Interaction between Cancer Cells and the Stroma
claim: Among the most highly up-regulated genes were members of the CXC/CC chemokine family including MCP-1 (CCL2), interleukin-(IL)-8 (CXCL8), GRO1 (CXCL1), and GRO2 (CXCL2); all of which have been implicated in tumor invasion and angiogenesis.

evidence.quote: USP5 stabilized STAT3 via its deubiquitination function, thereby enhancing the production of pro-angiogenic factors by cancer cells, including VEGF, ANGPT2, and CXCL1.
evidence.note: one instance: CXCL1 listed as pro-angiogenic factor; other chemokines and invasion not addressed.

evidence.quote: IHC and duplex ISH revealed the distribution of the major cell types and CCL2-expressing endothelial cells and fibroblasts, indicating tumor invasion.
evidence.note: one instance: CCL2-expressing cells indicate tumor invasion; angiogenesis and other chemokines not addressed.

module: 14.2 Interaction between Cancer Cells and the Stroma
claim: CAF-derived lactate is crucial in prostate cancer metabolic transformation towards OXPHOS.

evidence.quote: In prostate cancer (PCa), cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) are major contributors of secreted lactate, able to impact on metabolic and transcriptional regulation in cancer cells.
evidence.note: CAF lactate affects prostate cancer cell metabolism; OXPHOS shift not stated.

module: 14.2 Interaction between Cancer Cells and the Stroma
claim: The stroma can form up to 90% of the tumor volume, a property which is unique to pancreatic cancer.

evidence.quote: However, the epithelia-derived cancer component forms only a relatively small fraction of the tumor mass. The majority of the tumor consists of acellular fibrous stroma and diverse populations of the non-neoplastic cancer-associated cells.
evidence.note: Pancreatic tumor mass is mostly stroma; no 90% figure and no comparison with other cancer types.

module: 14.2 Interaction between Cancer Cells and the Stroma
claim: Transcription growth factor-alpha and beta (TGF-A and TGF-B), platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF), granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), epidermal growth factor (EGF), and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) all have implications in fibroblast regulation.

evidence.quote: In addition, stromal fibroblast cell autonomous effects have been observed in response to TGF-beta stimulation.
evidence.note: one instance: TGF-beta affects stromal fibroblasts; other listed factors not addressed.

claim: Activation of MMPs in the tumour microenvironment promotes tumour cell migration and invasion, release of sequestered growth factors, and activation of latent forms of cytokines including IL-1β.

evidence.quote: Matrix metalloprotease-3 (MMP-3), a zinc-dependent endopeptidase, degrades several extracellular substrates and contributes to local invasion by creating a microenvironment suitable for tumor development.
evidence.note: MMP-3 promotes local invasion; growth factor release and cytokine activation not stated.

claim: Constitutive activation of NF-κB and STAT3 is found in several human tumours, and these factors act synergistically to sustain and enhance tumour-associated inflammation.

evidence.quote: In the colorectal cancer (CRC) niche, the transcription factors signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) are hyperactivated in both malignant cells and tumor-infiltrating leukocytes (TILs) and cooperate to maintain cancer cell proliferation/survival and drive protumor inflammation.
evidence.note: one instance: STAT3 and NF-κB hyperactivated and cooperating in colorectal cancer, driving protumor inflammation.

evidence.quote: Recently, roles of NF-κB and STAT3 in colon, gastric and liver cancers have been extensively investigated. The activation and interaction between STAT3 and NF-κB play vital roles in control of the communication between cancer cells and inflammatory cells.
evidence.note: NF-κB/STAT3 interaction studied in several cancers; constitutive activation and synergy in inflammation not explicitly stated.

claim: IL-23 is a key cytokine in tumour growth and invasion; it causes upregulation of MMP-9 expression and increases angiogenesis and fibrosis.

evidence.quote: The level of the proinflammatory cytokine IL-6 and the expression of IL-23 in tumors of IL-12 KO mice were markedly higher than in the tumors of WT mice. IL-23 has been shown to promote tumor growth.
evidence.note: States IL-23 promotes tumor growth; MMP-9, angiogenesis and fibrosis effects of IL-23 not stated.

claim: IL-6 also promotes tumour angiogenesis and invasion.

evidence.quote: For this reason, such cytokines influence key parameters of oncogenesis, increasing cell resistance to apoptosis, proliferation of cancer cells, angiogenesis, invasion and malignancy as well as the ability of tumor cells to respond to anticancer therapy.
evidence.note: Review says IL-1 and IL-6 increase angiogenesis and invasion in cancer. Strict re-read: the quote does not state IL-6 not named; only 'such cytokines' generally.

claim: Key cytokines in tumour-associated inflammation are IL-1 and tumour necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α).

evidence.quote: Interleukin 1 beta (IL-1β) and Tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) are key inflammatory cytokines whose polymorphisms have been correlated with increased susceptibility to gastric cancer (GC).
evidence.note: Calls IL-1β and TNF-α key inflammatory cytokines linked to gastric cancer risk; tumour-associated inflammation not directly described.

claim: An important and almost immediate consequence of VEGF-A action is leakage of plasma proteins, including fibrinogen and other clotting factors.

evidence.quote: On the other hand, VPF/VEGF renders these same microvascular ECs hyperpermeable so that they spill plasma proteins into the extravascular space, leading to the clotting of extravasated fibrinogen with deposition of a fibrin gel.
evidence.note: VEGF causes plasma protein spillage and fibrinogen clotting; 'almost immediate' timing not stated here. Strict re-read: the quote does not state 'Almost immediate' timing and clotting factors beyond fibrinogen not stated.

claim: Various aggressive subtypes of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF) identified in numerous cancers include antigen-presenting CAFs (apCAFs), inflammatory CAFs (iCAFs), and myofibroblastic CAFs (myCAFs).

evidence.quote: We corroborate the presence of myofibroblastic CAFs and inflammatory CAFs and define their unique gene signatures in vivo. Moreover, we describe a new population of CAFs that express MHC class II and CD74, but do not express classic costimulatory molecules.
evidence.note: one instance: myCAF, iCAF and antigen-presenting CAFs described in pancreatic cancer; 'aggressive' not stated.

evidence.quote: Single-cell RNA sequencing segregates CAF into inflammatory and growth factor-enriched (iCAF) and myofibroblastic (myCAF) subpopulations, displaying distinct ligand-receptor interactions.
evidence.note: one instance: iCAF and myCAF subtypes in cholangiocarcinoma; apCAF not mentioned.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: A small number of CSCs can reconstruct the entire cancer tissue hierarchy, leading to recurrence after surgery or therapy.

evidence.quote: Despite the small number of such cells, they might be the cause of tumor recurrence, sometimes many years after the "successful" treatment of primary tumor.
evidence.note: Small number of CSCs might cause recurrence; regenerating the full hierarchy not stated here.

evidence.quote: PDX chemotherapy results in CSC resistance and expansion, also seen in recurrent patient GBM.
evidence.note: Links CSC resistance and expansion to GBM recurrence; no cell number or hierarchy regeneration.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: At the bottom tier are the most differentiated cancer cells, which comprise the bulk of the tumor mass.

evidence.quote: Within the microenvironment, CSC self-renewal, replication, and differentiation are postulated to produce a hierarchy of cells constituting the tumor mass.
evidence.note: Hierarchy of differentiated cells makes up the tumor mass; bottom tier and bulk proportion not stated.

evidence.quote: While cytotoxic chemotherapy kills the bulk of tumor cells, CSCs are spared and have the ability to recapitulate the heterogenic tumor mass.
evidence.note: Mentions bulk tumor cells versus CSCs; not the bottom tier of the hierarchy.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: At the top tier are the CSCs themselves—a relatively small population of cells with unlimited self-renewal capacity.

evidence.quote: Previously coined "cancer stem cells" (CSCs) and believed to be a rare population with rigid hierarchical organization, there is good evidence to suggest that these cells exhibit a plastic cellular state influenced by dynamic CSC-niche interplay.
evidence.note: Says CSCs were believed rare but now seen as plastic; no unlimited self-renewal stated.

evidence.quote: Leukemia stem cells (LSC) reside within a hierarchy of malignant hematopoiesis and possess the ability to instigate, maintain and serially propagate leukemia in vivo, while retaining the capacity to differentiate into committed progeny that lack these properties.
evidence.note: Leukemia-specific: stem cells in hierarchy propagate serially; size not stated.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: Genetic studies performed over 20 years ago demonstrated that the malignant clone in CML is a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell, capable of differentiating into myeloid cells, monocytes, erythrocytes, and platelets.

evidence.quote: Chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) originates in a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell of the bone marrow and is characterized by greatly increased numbers of granulocytes in the blood. Myeloid and other hematopoietic cell lineages are involved in the process of clonal proliferation and differentiation.
evidence.note: CML originates in a pluripotent hematopoietic stem cell; myeloid and other lineages are involved. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Differentiation into monocytes, erythrocytes, platelets and early genetic studies not stated.

evidence.quote: Well established features of chronic phase CML are its origin in a pluripotent stem cell, a now well defined molecular genetic basis involving the creation of a BCR-ABL fusion gene and evidence of resultant abnormalities in the mechanisms that normally control primitive hemopoietic cell proliferation.
evidence.note: States chronic phase CML originates in a pluripotent stem cell. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Genetic studies over 20 years ago and differentiation into specific lineages not stated.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: In acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the CD34+CD38− marker combination was used to identify AML CSC, and the same combination also identifies normal HSCs.

evidence.quote: LSC containing CD34+CD38- fractions were measured using flow cytometry in an add-on study of the HOVON102/SAKK trial.
evidence.note: CD34+CD38- fractions contain AML LSCs; no statement that normal HSCs share this phenotype.

evidence.quote: In vitro assays showed that suppression of NCOA4 was toxic to leukemic blasts, particularly the CD34+CD38- LSC-enriched population, without affecting normal CD34+ hematopoietic progenitors.
evidence.note: CD34+CD38- is LSC-enriched; normal CD34+ progenitors mentioned but no shared-marker statement.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: In breast cancer, the hierarchy includes CD44+/CD24− mesenchymal-like cells at the top, which differentiate into ALDH+ epithelial-like intermediate cells, which in turn give rise to more differentiated bulk tumor cells.

evidence.quote: Here we identify XIST as a key regulator of breast cancer stem cells (CSCs), which exhibit aldehyde dehydrogenase positive (ALDH+) epithelial- (E) and CD24loCD44hi mesenchymal-like (M) phenotypes.
evidence.note: Names ALDH+ epithelial-like and CD24loCD44hi mesenchymal-like CSC phenotypes; no hierarchy order stated.

evidence.quote: Identification of BCSCs from tumor samples or breast cancer cell lines has been based mainly on CD44(+)/CD24(-/low) or ALDH(+) phenotypes.
evidence.note: Gives the two BCSC marker phenotypes only; no differentiation order.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: In pancreatic cancer, several CSC markers such as CD24/CD44/ESA triple positive or CD133 are identified and these CSC fractions revealed higher tumorigenicity, metastatic capability.

evidence.quote: These pancreatic cancer stem cells express the cell surface markers CD44, CD24, and epithelial-specific antigen, and represent 0.5% to 1.0% of all pancreatic cancer cells.
evidence.note: Gives CD44/CD24/ESA markers for pancreatic CSCs; no CD133, tumorigenicity or metastasis comparison here.

evidence.quote: Cancer stem cells (CSCs), which are pluripotent, self-renewable, and capable of forming tumors, contribute to PDAC initiation and metastasis and are responsible for resistance to chemotherapy and radiation.
evidence.note: CSCs form tumors and contribute to PDAC metastasis; markers listed elsewhere in the record, not higher-than-other fractions.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: In solid tumors, CSCs were initially identified in breast cancer (BCa) using a CD44+CD24− marker combination; these CD44+CD24− cells were purified from BCa samples using FACS and shown to possess stem cell properties.

evidence.quote: Breast cancer stem cells (BCSCs) constitute a subpopulation of tumor cells that express stem cell-associated markers and have a high capacity for tumor generation in vivo. Identification of BCSCs from tumor samples or breast cancer cell lines has been based mainly on CD44(+)/CD24(-/low) or ALDH(+) phenotypes.
evidence.note: CD44+/CD24-/low is a main BCSC marker with tumor-generating capacity; first identification and FACS not stated.

evidence.quote: Breast cancer stem cells, identified on the basis of CD44+CD24-/low expression, are associated with metastases and drug resistance.
evidence.note: BCSCs identified by CD44+CD24-/low; no first-isolation or FACS-purification stem property data.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: Side population cells from pancreatic cancer cell lines also contain CSC fraction evidenced by increased tumorigenicity and chemoresistance.

evidence.quote: Using orthotopic xenografts into the severely immunocompromised NSG mouse, we found that SP cells isolated from both cell lines produced tumors that were highly metastatic, in contrast to previous experience with PDAC cell lines.
evidence.note: Panc-1 and BxPC3 SP cells formed highly metastatic tumors; supports tumorigenicity, not compared to non-SP cells.

evidence.quote: The sensitivity of PDAC SP cells to the vinca alkaloid vincristine could be greatly increased by verapamil, a general inhibitor of transporters. In contrast, verapamil had no effect on the killing of PDAC cells by gemcitabine, the current first-line therapeutic for PDAC.
evidence.note: Describes SP cell drug-resistance via transporters; mixed result, resistance to gemcitabine not conferred by ABCG2.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: Side population (SP), a marker-independent strategy, was originally used to enrich normal HSC and leukemia SC but was later used extensively to enrich CSCs in several solid tumors.

evidence.quote: Previous studies have demonstrated SP cells in bone marrow obtained from patients with acute myeloid leukemia, suggesting that these cells might be candidate leukemic stem cells, and recent studies have found a SP of tumor progenitor cells in human solid tumors.
evidence.note: SP cells in AML marrow and in solid tumors; normal hematopoietic stem cell use and order not stated.

evidence.quote: We used flow cytometry and the DNA-binding dye (Hoechst 33342) to isolate side population (SP) cells from various human gastrointestinal system cancer cell lines.
evidence.note: one instance: SP isolation used in gastrointestinal cancer cell lines.

module: 15.1 Concept and Characteristics of Cancer Stem Cells
claim: The ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter family proteins such as MDR1 and ABCG2 are responsible for dye exclusion and the side population phenotypic profile.

evidence.quote: The efflux of Hoechst 33342 by ATP-binding cassette protein G2 (ABCG2) membrane pump allows reproducible identification of a subpopulation of cells by flow cytometric analysis termed the "side population" (SP).
evidence.note: ABCG2 efflux of Hoechst defines the SP; MDR1 not mentioned.

evidence.quote: Side population (SP) sorting using an ultraviolet (UV) laser is an established method to isolate CSC based on ABC drug transporter-dependent (e.g., ABCG2) Hoechst 33342 efflux.
evidence.note: SP phenotype depends on ABC drug transporters such as ABCG2 via Hoechst efflux. Strict re-read: the quote does not state MDR1 and side population phenotype link not stated; only ABCG2 efflux.

claim: As a tumor expands or develops metastasis, these clones would compete for survival, leading to clonal evolution of a given lesion or host.

evidence.quote: Evolution and natural selection of tumoral clones in the process of transformation and the following carcinogenesis can be called natural clonal evolution.
evidence.note: Natural selection among tumoral clones is termed clonal evolution; competition on expansion/metastasis not explicit. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Clones competing for survival upon tumor expansion/metastasis not stated.

evidence.quote: Tumour cells are subjected to evolutionary selection pressures during progression from initiation to metastasis.
evidence.note: Selection pressures act through progression to metastasis; competition wording not used.

claim: Intratumoral heterogeneity, referring to the variations among different tumor lesions and/or tumor cells within a single patient, is largely driven by genomic instability.

evidence.quote: Genome doubling and ongoing dynamic chromosomal instability were associated with intratumor heterogeneity and resulted in parallel evolution of driver somatic copy-number alterations, including amplifications in CDK4, FOXA1, and BCL11A.
evidence.note: Chromosomal instability associated with intratumor heterogeneity in NSCLC; association, not stated as the main driver.

evidence.quote: We emphasize the importance of macro-evolutionary leaps, often involving large-scale chromosomal alterations, in driving tumor evolution and metastasis
evidence.note: Large-scale chromosomal alterations drive tumor evolution; heterogeneity not directly tied to genomic instability.

claim: On the other hand, the CSC theory states that a significant source of heterogeneity in cancer cells is due to CSCs, which are undifferentiated and have high rates of division.

evidence.quote: Glioblastomas display striking cellular heterogeneity, with stem-like glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) at the apex.
evidence.note: Glioblastoma heterogeneity with stem-like cells at the apex; not explicit as a source of heterogeneity or rapid division.

evidence.quote: We also find that this progenitor population contains the majority of the cancer's cycling cells, and, using RNA velocity, is often the originator of the other cell types.
evidence.note: Progenitor cancer stem cells hold most cycling cells and originate other cell types in glioblastoma.

claim: The clonal evolution theory claims that genetically and metabolically distinct subpopulations arise from a previously larger population of cancer cells due to the expansion of the population, genetic diversification, and selection of certain subclones over others.

evidence.quote: Clonal evolution of a tumor ecosystem depends on different selection pressures that are principally immune and treatment mediated.
evidence.note: Clonal evolution shaped by selection pressures; expansion and diversification of subclones not described.

evidence.quote: Fortuitously however, the cancer genome, by virtue of ongoing mutations that uniquely mark clonal lineages within the tumour, provides a rich, yet surreptitious, record of cancer development.
evidence.note: Mutations mark clonal lineages recording tumor development; no definition of the clonal evolution model.

claim: Unstable genome in tumor cells leads to the occurrence of a wide range of mutations and, as such, fosters genetic diversity and the generation of genetically different cancer cell clones.

evidence.quote: We emphasize the importance of macro-evolutionary leaps, often involving large-scale chromosomal alterations, in driving tumor evolution and metastasis and consider the role of the tumor microenvironment in engendering heterogeneity and drug resistance.
evidence.note: Large-scale chromosomal alterations drive tumor evolution; genome instability generating distinct clones not stated explicitly.

evidence.quote: This heterogeneity might result in a non-uniform distribution of genetically distinct tumour-cell subpopulations across and within disease sites (spatial heterogeneity) or temporal variations in the molecular makeup of cancer cells (temporal heterogeneity).
evidence.note: Describes genetically distinct tumour-cell subpopulations; no link to genomic instability stated.

claim: A distinct gene signature associated with tumorigenic CD24−/low/CD44+ cell populations correlates with shorter distant metastasis-free and overall survival, suggesting that presence and frequency of this cell population has prognostic relevance.

evidence.quote: There was a significant association between the IGS and both overall and metastasis-free survival (P<0.001, for both) in patients with breast cancer, which was independent of established clinical and pathological variables.
evidence.note: Signature from CD44+CD24-/low cells is significantly associated with survival outcomes; direction (shorter survival) not explicitly stated.

claim: Activation of the STAT3 pathway through IL-6 results in trastuzumab resistance and an increase in HER2-positive cells in breast CSCs, suggesting that targeting this pathway could restore treatment sensitivity.

evidence.quote: The results suggest that CAFs induce trastuzumab resistance by expanding cancer stem cells and activating multiple pathways, such as NF-κB, JAK/STAT3 and PI3K/AKT; combination of an anti-IL6 antibody, or multiple pathway inhibitors with trastuzumab in HER2 positive breast cancer maybe a novel strategy to reverse trastuzumab resistance.
evidence.note: CAFs induce resistance via CSC expansion and JAK/STAT3 activation; IL-6 and HER2-positive cell increase not directly stated.

evidence.quote: Continued use of trastuzumab in HER2(+) PTEN(-) cells increased the frequency of cancer stem cells (CSCs) and metastasis potential.
evidence.note: Trastuzumab resistance increased CSC frequency; not attributed to IL-6/STAT3 activation.

claim: Activation of the transcription factor FOXA1 in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer treated with osimertinib results in upregulated expression of IGF-1R.

evidence.quote: The tolerance is mediated by the increased expression and phosphorylation of insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor (IGF-1R), caused by the induction of its transcription factor FOXA1.
evidence.note: IGF-1R increase in osimertinib tolerance is caused by induction of FOXA1. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Osimertinib and EGFR-mutant NSCLC not named in quote.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts create a chemoresistant niche through increased secretion of specific cytokines and chemokines.

evidence.quote: Cytokines, growth factors, and extracellular vesicles create paracrine loops that promote radio- and chemoresistance through activation of pro-survival signaling pathways.
evidence.note: Cytokines in the tumour microenvironment (with CAFs) promote chemoresistance; CAF secretion not specifically attributed.

evidence.quote: Overall, these findings indicate that a proinflammatory niche created by the interplay between SCC and CAF triggers tumor progression.
evidence.note: Cytokine-driven niche of cancer cells and CAFs drives progression after chemotherapy; chemoresistance not stated.

claim: Cancer-associated fibroblasts secrete many growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines, including hepatocyte growth factor, which activates MET receptors to protect CSCs from apoptosis in response to cetuximab monotherapy targeting EGFR in metastatic colorectal cancer.

evidence.quote: Addition of HGF to cetuximab-treated cells phosphorylated MET, but not EGFR or ErbB3, restimulated the MAPK and AKT pathways, restored cell proliferation, and rescued cells from G1 arrest and apoptosis.
evidence.note: HGF via MET rescues cetuximab-treated CRC cells from apoptosis; HGF was added exogenously, no CAF source or stem-cell focus stated.

claim: CAR-T cells are being developed to target CSC markers such as CD133, CD44, EpCAM, and combinations thereof.

evidence.quote: A Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating the Safety and Preliminary Efficacy of CD44/CD133 Dual-Target Tris-CAR-T Cell Therapy in Patients With Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma
evidence.note: one instance: CD44/CD133 dual-target CAR-T trial; dated: status not yet recruiting, start 2026-10-15. Strict re-read: the quote does not state EpCAM and CSC-targeting framing not stated; only CD44/CD133 CAR-T trial.

evidence.quote: The Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cells (CAR-T) that target TM4SF1 or EpCAM have been generated respectively in our good manufacturing practices (GMP) facility and their anti-tumor effects have been demonstrated in multiple in vitro and in vivo studies.
evidence.note: one instance: EpCAM-targeted CAR-T clinical study; dated: trial status UNKNOWN, started 2019. Strict re-read: the quote does not state CD133, CD44 as CSC targets; quote covers TM4SF1/EpCAM CAR-T.

claim: CD10+/GPR77+ cancer-associated fibroblasts promote tumor formation and chemoresistance by providing a niche for CSC survival.

evidence.quote: Moreover, CCL18 secreted by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) activated a CD10+GPR77+ CAF phenotype in normal breast-resident fibroblasts (NBFs), which could then enrich cancer stem cells (CSCs) and induce chemoresistance in breast cancer cells.
evidence.note: CD10+GPR77+ CAFs enrich cancer stem cells and induce chemoresistance in breast cancer. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Tumor formation and CSC survival niche not stated.

evidence.quote: CD10 and GPR77 define a cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) subset that sustains cancer stemness.
evidence.note: CD10/GPR77 CAF subset sustains cancer stemness; chemoresistance not stated in this text.

claim: CD13+ hepatocellular CSCs predominate in the G0 phase of the cell cycle and exhibit resistance to 5-fluorouracil treatment, as the mechanism of 5-fluorouracil primarily involves inhibition of DNA replication.

evidence.quote: CD13+ cells predominated in the G0 phase of the cell cycle and typically formed cellular clusters in cancer foci.
evidence.note: Supports the G0 predominance of CD13+ liver CSCs; says nothing here on 5-FU resistance.

evidence.quote: 5-FU inhibited CD90+ proliferating CSCs, some of which produce CD13+ semiquiescent CSCs, while CD13 inhibition suppressed the self-renewing and tumor-initiating ability of dormant CSCs.
evidence.note: 5-FU hits proliferating CD90+ CSCs, not CD13+ semiquiescent ones; DNA-replication mechanism not stated.

claim: CD133+ HCC cells isolated from human cell lines and xenograft mouse models are resistant to chemotherapeutics through activation of Akt/PKB and Bcl-2 pathways.

evidence.quote: In this study, we found that CD133+ HepG2 and Huh7 cells were resistant to cisplatin treatment, compared to the CD133- HepG2 and Huh7 cells.
evidence.note: CD133+ HCC cell lines resist cisplatin; xenograft models and mechanism not stated here.

evidence.quote: As a result, osthole inhibited the phosphorylation of AKT and Bad to decrease the amount of free Bcl-2 in CD133+ HepG2 and Huh7 cells.
evidence.note: Links AKT/Bad/Bcl-2 to CD133+ HCC resistance indirectly, via osthole inhibition rather than stating Akt/Bcl-2 activation as the cause.

claim: CD44 expression suppresses ferroptosis in cancer cells, indicating a correlation between CSCs and ferroptosis.

evidence.quote: MEN1 facilitated lipid ROS generation and sensitized lung cancer cells to ferroptosis by perturbing CD44 precursor messenger RNA splicing.
evidence.note: Altering CD44 splicing sensitizes lung cancer cells to ferroptosis; CD44 suppressing ferroptosis only implied.

evidence.quote: Collectively, these findings suggest that platycodin D attenuates ferroptosis in GCs by activating CD44/SLC7A11 axis, thereby upregulating system Xc-.
evidence.note: CD44 activation attenuates ferroptosis, but in ovarian granulosa cells, not cancer cells.

claim: CD44 expression suppresses ferroptosis in cancer cells, indicating correlation between CSCs and ferroptosis.

evidence.note: Activating CD44 attenuates ferroptosis, but in ovarian granulosa cells (PCOS), not cancer cells.

evidence.quote: Furthermore, CD44 variable exon 6-interfering peptides effectively abrogated the growth and metastasis of established MEN1-deficient tumors by activating ferroptosis.
evidence.note: Interfering with CD44 variant exon 6 activates ferroptosis in lung tumours; CD44 expression effect only implied.

claim: CD80 subsequently binds to CTLA-4, thereby suppressing cytotoxicity of cytotoxic T lymphocytes.

evidence.quote: (Microbial infection) Interacts with Orthopoxvirus OPG038/M2 protein, inhibiting the interaction with CTLA4/CD152
evidence.note: Implies CD80 interacts with CTLA4 (viral protein blocks it); nothing on effect on T-cell cytotoxicity.

claim: Chemotherapy such as oxaliplatin induces Notch-1 receptor and its downstream target Hes-1 activity by increasing gamma-secretase activity in colon cancer cells.

evidence.quote: We then report that chemotherapy induces Notch-1, as oxaliplatin, 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), or SN-38 (the active metabolite of irinotecan) induced Notch-1 intracellular domain (NICD) protein and activated Hes-1.
evidence.note: Oxaliplatin induced Notch-1 intracellular domain and activated Hes-1 in colon cancer cells. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Increase in gamma-secretase activity as mechanism not stated; colon cancer not stated.

evidence.quote: Induction of NICD by oxaliplatin was caused by an increase in the activity and expression of gamma-secretase complex, as suppression of the protein subunit nicastrin with small interfering RNA (siRNA) prevented NICD induction after oxaliplatin.
evidence.note: Oxaliplatin-induced NICD was caused by increased gamma-secretase activity and expression. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Hes-1 and colon cancer cells not stated; only NICD induction by oxaliplatin via gamma-secretase.

claim: Cisplatin pretreatment in cells contributes to the interaction of histone deacetylase and TRIB1, which is overexpressed in leukemia and together inactivates p53.

evidence.quote: Interestingly, cisplatin treatment also contributed to the increasement of HDAC, the interaction of TRIB1 with HDAC, and inactivation of p53.
evidence.note: Cisplatin increased TRIB1-HDAC interaction and p53 inactivation, in NSCLC cells rather than leukemia. Strict re-read: the quote does not state Leukemia and TRIB1 overexpression not stated.

claim: Combining oncolytic viruses with mesenchymal stem cells increases treatment effectiveness and reduces side effects because of the ability of mesenchymal stem cells to reach tumors quickly.

evidence.quote: Due to their inherent tumor tropism mesenchymal stem cells loaded with oncolytic virus can improve delivery of the therapeutic cargo to cancer sites. Shielding of oncolytic viral construct from antiviral host immune response makes these cells prospective delivery vehicles to even hard-to-reach metastatic neoplastic foci.
evidence.note: MSC tumour tropism improves oncolytic virus delivery; reduced side effects not stated.

evidence.quote: Administration of OV-loaded MSCs with radiotherapy to mice bearing brainstem DIPG xenografts results in more prolonged survival relative to that conferred by either therapy alone (P < 0.01).
evidence.note: OV-loaded MSCs plus radiotherapy prolonged survival in mouse DIPG model; no side-effect finding.
